speaker: donanderson
text: I'd like to, on behalf of the city of Lakewood, call the Lakewood City Council into session for our joint meeting with the Clover Park School Board for January 25th, 2021. Board Chair.

speaker: martyschafer
text: And I would acknowledge the Clover Park School District is going to officially call our joint meeting with the City Council to order as well. And with that, we have full attendance.

speaker: donanderson
text: As do we, it's a great pleasure that we could all get together, including our CEOs here, and discuss some things. I see from the agenda that I'm up. The first item we'd like to go over is what Lakewood is doing with respect to the Lakewood Business Park and what's going on there as a result of our city initiatives and the Clover Park School District's disposition of property. Just a little bit of background. Currently, there's 188 acres zone light industrial and more than 2 million square feet of light industrial manufacturing property, even either built or currently under construction. This is meeting what's been a tremendous need for light industrial distribution and warehousing along the I-5 corridor, along with light manufacturing. Our economy's changing. COVID accelerated that. It didn't change the general trajectory, but it did certainly change the pace at which the economy has changed. This creates hundreds of jobs for Pierce County, including family wage jobs, and it also had the salutary effect of cleaning up brought light. It was done in a manner that provided this relocation assistance to individuals, to areas with more adequate service. The Port of Tacoma was a partner with us. They essentially had run out of property in Fredrickson, and we're looking for partners to help facilitate growth in Pierce County, which would enable the continuation, expansion of port traffic. And so they helped along with others in creating this opportunity for economic development. So far, there's been an estimate of $220 million of private sector investment in property and improvements in this area. And if we have some graphics here that if Ms. Schumacher could screen share, go back and show you how the transformation has taken place. If you haven't been out there recently, you really should take a look because if you've been away for six months, you wouldn't recognize some of it. See how big we can get that. So back in 2000 and 2001, the city created 117 and a half acre industrially zoned area in Woodbrook in its comprehensive plan and zoning. The purpose was to stimulate, stimulate, I said, sewer extension too, and jobs in the area. And it was instrumental in gaining funding for sewer extensions. The sewer extensions were actually done by the city of Lakewood and not by the sewer utility, which is quite unusual. Grants and some other funding opportunities arose along with some availability charges that allowed us to piecemeal this together and provide the sewer trunk lines in this previously unsewered area. 20 acres of the property, basically across the street from the Woodbrook Middle School site had been assembled by a, were assembled after that by a single entity in anticipation of a development community. I was told it took them about 10 years to put that together. So if we move on to 2008, that's when the Port of Tacoma partnered with the city of Lakewood to fund the Woodbrook Business Park redevelopment report. And this key partnership prepared for an industrial expansion. So in July of 2009, the report was published and its main conclusion was that right-of-way improvements needed to be paid. The middle school needed to be relocated. Sewer needed to be extended. And work needed to be done with housing agencies to relocate the lowest income units to other housing areas which provided more adequate services to those who live there. Work with WSDOT on the Crossbate Highway through Fort Lewis at that time was suggested and that has since been suspended. There's no funding on the horizon that anticipates that project will be completed. The recommendations also included recommendation to implement landscaping and streetscaping to make a business park more attractive and to provide fencing and a buffer for any adjacent residential zone areas. In 2011, the Pioneer came and that's the blue arrow. That was Olympic Moving and Storage completed a new building and it was probably the first new building out there in decades. Extended the underlying zoning and the underlying zoning was extended to include Woodbrook Middle School site which was a prior non-conforming use. So it was allowed to continue under the zoning but it was set the stage for that being able to be industrially developed. And in 2012, phase one of the sewer extension was completed. So moving forward in 2015, the city was very active in supporting the I-5 JBLM Congestion Relief Transportation Improvement Project. The big mess you see going on between Lakewood and what's now Lewis, Maine. And that created a new interchange at I-5 leading into Woodbrook at the Thorne Lane exit. That was designed with the idea that it would facilitate freight traffic in and out of the business park. We will continue to work with you on facilities and supported the new man middle school now Claudia Thomas Middle School as an enhancement replacement of Clover Park's Woodbrook facilities. So in move forward on the slides, that's the right one. In 2016 permits were submitted for the 467,000 square foot Panatoni warehouse across from the Woodbrook site. That's on the area that had been so long anticipated as a development site. And in phase in 2017, the phase one of the sewer project was completed. We, I think that's when we were enabled to complete a loop and the warehouse was completed. And at that point, multiple properties came on the market. So in 2018, we extended the industrial business park zoning another 31 and a half acres, expanding it to the present 188 acres and completed the sewer extension from Woodbrook to the East 150th. The 467,000 square foot warehouse was leased to Damco and Geodes and Black Creek properties purchased the Clover Park school district properties. Emerson Lake business park was established and that has a SEPA in progress. The new interchange design build was in progress and a new project at 146th and Woodbrook Drive was in process, the American Lakewood Logistics. A new project South of 150th and Woodbrook Drive is also in process. So a lot started happening in 2018 and people started to consolidate properties out there. So if we go forward to much the present, I think it was our last slide. It's a little bit harder to see from a big angle, but in 2019-20, the first building was completed by Black Creek on former Clover Park school district property South of 150th and Spring Street. Construction started on other Black Creek buildings and is currently moving forward for more. Also in progress are the American Lake Logistics property and a property South of 150th and Woodbrook Drive. The private sewer extension has taken place from 150th on 150th from Spring Street to the West by Black Creek. And if you drive out there today, in addition to the various properties that are springing up, you'll also see a variety of commercial real estate signs indicating that development properties are for sale. And so this is where we sit today and that 188 acres is fast filling up, providing jobs and economic stability for the city, pretty good tax base for the school district. And really the linchpin in all this was going back to when the city decided that it would take the initiative to extend sewer to that area because development could not take place without it. We're actually failing septic systems. In fact, there still are some failing septic systems in that area that are not hooked up to the school. So that's the reason we brought along John Caulfield is if you folks from the school district have any questions, he's the guy that has the answers. So I invite any questions. That's a pretty, you know, 50,000 foot overview of what's going on out there. But there's, one of the things that actually happened in the process here was that I heard at least one of the projects was slowed down a little bit because of the shortage of concrete because they were using it all to repave the runway at McCord. So it's interesting that so much was going on in our neighborhood at the same time.

It's kind of sad that we really want this school up and running and we're hoping to get a student in-person friendly as soon as possible, of course. On the funding side, again, I just wanna acknowledge that this is the seventh school constructed by Clover Park School District since 2013 without asking the taxpayers to fund that capital project. I know I'm repeating myself, but I've been on the school board now for 15 years and we've worked with many other school districts. It's an anomaly to have that many buildings erected, especially without having an excessive levy or campaigns on the community. So it was quite a right accomplishment. The building itself came around the $76 million mark. At this point, it is expected to come under budget. So we're thankful for that. The highlights of the facility is that the building itself is 131,599 square feet. It has 21.4 acres, so it's not quite as large as what we had in Woodbrook, but it is quite capable for housing the 1,000 to 1,500 students that it can house, or I'm sorry, 1,000 to 1,150 students. It's basically also serving some of the fields to where there's a restroom facilities that can be used for those activities as well. It has three science classrooms per grade, resource rooms, music choir, band rooms, CTE rooms, art, a media center, computer labs, a raised stage platform facing the commons, and a full prep kitchen. There are also rooms for life skills, success and FT, as well as a main and auxiliary gym with associated locker rooms. Again, it is state-of-the-art and we're very proud of it. The site also has three tennis courts and all-weather running track surrounding a football field. It has two baseball, softball fields, public and staff parking areas, and a bus loop that is separated from parent drop-off pickup lanes. And it is nestled in a quiet neighborhood as well. So it's a fantastic school and we're expecting that it's gonna serve our students and really future generations very well. So we're excited for it. speaker: donanderson
text: So the next item of the agenda is an equity discussion. And I am not sure who has the lead on this.

speaker: martyschafer
text: Well, we would turn that over to our superintendent to be able to give an overview on some of what we're calling our equity journey. I think it's important to acknowledge that we began a very focused opportunity to grow in the area of equity and create a policy that would be living and moving. And so it goes back really to about the year 2004, but in the last couple of years, we've been very concentrated on it and made a lot of progress. So superintendent Banner, anything that you can share on our scope of action for the equity would be wonderful.

speaker: ronbanner
text: Sure, thank you, directors and council persons. Just in regards to our equity journey, as President Schaffer described, we as a district back to 2004 initiated an equity and excellence policy, and it was reaffirmed in 2012. And what we've done is embarked on what we call a deep dive in our equity work. And so that dive includes staff development, professional development for our staff. A lot of this is looking at what we bring to the table as opposed to looking out the window. We call that looking in the mirror as opposed to looking out the window and really identifying self-awareness, what we bring to the table, what we bring to our students so that we know how to best serve our students and families. We're also working towards empowering student voice. So often we negate asking our students simple things like what would make this school better? What would make this district better? What would make this class better to help serve and encourage learning? And so we're working to empower student voice also to empower families who haven't necessarily felt enfranchised. We're working to empower them so that their voice matters. We have recently embarked on policy development to address probably what I would call the inefficiencies of a previous policy in today's day. And our board has approved as of Saturday as to move forward in policy development and looking at the timeline for that, which would be about a six to eight month process before we presented something for final adoption. And that would include massive amounts of stakeholder input with continual touchstones back to the board of directors on Saturday, the board put together through some small group work and activities, just the basic elements that they would like to see in a policy. And so we'll begin there with our board helping to create that from the ground up as it should be. That's the basic overview of our work. There are many, many things that we're doing. We are a primary piece of our work has been collaboration with the city, city manager Caulfield and I met with along with a couple of folks from our teams, respective teams. And we just said, hey, what's happening and how can we work together to improve both of our organizations in terms of equity. And I think both the board and the council person saw a joint letter from city manager Caulfield and I probably about early fall. And we continue to meet on a regular basis, not just John and I meet regularly, but we also will have additional meetings specifically around equity. And we're not trying to build a rocket ship here. It's really one of the basic things we can do to move this work forward. And we've had a few things come of that that were in the letter. So that being said, again, it's about a 50,000 foot view of our equity journey. I'm sure there's more details. And if there are any questions, I'd be happy to field those.

text: In general, what we hope to achieve is that families are taking a more active role because they believe that what they say matters and it will lead to actionable steps.
